decision: Each system is one case: the company in three lines, then one problem behind the scenes and one on the screen
why: A founder remembers a company and two decisions, not twenty components. The same shape repeats for Atlas and Pulse.
alternative: One architecture page per system with every component on it.
value: Anyone can say what the case is about after thirty seconds.

decision: The backend problem is framed as protecting sales per minute on Black Friday, not as handling more traffic
why: Every minute is worth a different amount; the architecture should protect the valuable ones first and cost what that protection is worth.
value: Every technical choice on the next page has a business number attached.

decision: The frontend problem keeps the existing static storefront and adds a thin live layer
why: The storefront is already fast, cheap and accessible; the gap is fast-changing truth (price, stock, the bag) and a designed busy mode.
alternative: Rebuild the storefront around server rendering for freshness.
value: Keeps what works and fixes only what it can't do.

decision: Only measured results appear as facts; every other number on the case pages is labeled illustrative
why: Credibility is the product of a portfolio; invented outcomes would undo it.
alternative: Plausible projected outcomes for each decision.
value: API latency 450 → ~200 ms and Uptime 99.5 → 99.9% stand on their own.

decision: The hub ends with the ten engineering concepts the case teaches, each in one line
why: The case is also a study map: the mechanism matters more than the product names.
value: Engineers see the depth; everyone else can skip it.
